source.title: Bidirectional Associations across Time between Entitativity, Positive Affect, Generosity, and Religiousness in Adolescents Training with a Religiously Affiliated Charity Marathon Team

paper.citation: Schnitker, S., Shubert, J., Houltberg, B., & Fernandez, N. (2020). Bidirectional associations across time between entitativity, positive affect, generosity, and religiousness in adolescents training with a religiously affiliated charity marathon team. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17(3), 686. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17030686
paper.abstract: How do intrinsic religiousness, group closeness, positive affect, self-reported generosity, and fundraising relate across pretraining, midtraining, and postrace measurement in a religious charity marathon program? The sample included 396 Team World Vision participants aged 12–22 years (mean 18.42); 63% were female and 88% identified with a Christian tradition. Only 227 participants (57%) provided data at all three waves. This was a voluntary, religiously affiliated charity half/full-marathon setting, not an elite or collegiate team-performance program. Exploratory 18-week longitudinal observational design with three survey waves and cross-lagged latent path analysis. Measures included perceived group entitativity, positive affect, intrinsic religiousness, and self-reported interpersonal generosity. Fundraising totals were treated as a candidate behavioral generosity proxy and categorized into quartiles, with socioeconomic status included as a covariate.
paper.tldr: This longitudinal observational study examines psychosocial development in a structured charitable endurance-training context, with indirect relevance to athlete culture and character formation. Higher pretraining generosity predicted greater positive affect during training, which in turn predicted higher postrace generosity. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Exploratory 18-week longitudinal observational design with three survey waves and cross-lagged latent path analysis. Measures included perceived group entitativity, positive affect, intrinsic religiousness, and self-reported interpersonal generosity. Fundraising totals were treated as a candidate behavioral generosity proxy and categorized into quartiles, with socioeconomic status included as a covariate.
paper.findings: Higher pretraining generosity predicted greater positive affect during training, which in turn predicted higher postrace generosity. Increased intrinsic religiousness during training was associated with higher postrace generosity. The model showed temporal associations, but the authors explicitly characterized the analysis as exploratory and did not claim experimental causation. Fundraising was not compellingly supported as a behavioral indicator of generosity, although midtraining generosity predicted postrace fundraising.
paper.limitations: No secular charity, non-athletic religious, or non-charity athletic control group was available, preventing attribution to running, team affiliation, charitable purpose, religion, or their combination. Attrition was high and may have selected participants on unmeasured health, motivation, or personality characteristics. Self-reported generosity may reflect socially desirable responding, particularly when religiousness and prosocial identity are salient. Fundraising depends on social networks and resources and is not equivalent to donating one's own resources or behaving generously. Generalization beyond a predominantly Christian, mostly White, recreational endurance-charity context is limited. Cross-lagged associations do not establish causal developmental effects.
paper.practicalImplications: The study supports asking how program context, shared purpose, positive emotion, and group connection develop together; it does not prove that endurance training or religious affiliation creates generosity. If applying the idea in collegiate sport, use voluntary, inclusive, athlete-centered programming and measure intended psychosocial outcomes directly. Do not use fundraising or religious participation as a character score.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. The study supports asking how program context, shared purpose, positive emotion, and group connection develop together; it does not prove that endurance training or religious affiliation creates generosity. If applying the idea in collegiate sport, use voluntary, inclusive, athlete-centered programming and measure intended psychosocial outcomes directly. Do not use fundraising or religious participation as a character score. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
